questions.question: Give four reasons why Timbuktu became a centre of learning.
questions.expected_answer: Wealth from trade supported scholars and bought books; Islam brought Arabic literacy and valued knowledge; rulers such as Mansa Musa and Askia Muhammad honoured and paid scholars; trade routes linked Timbuktu to centres of learning such as Fez, Cairo and Mecca, bringing books, paper and scholars; scholarly families had independence and authority in the city.

questions.question: Describe how a student was educated in Timbuktu, including the role of the ijaza.
questions.expected_answer: Children attended Quranic schools to learn Arabic letters on wooden boards and memorise the Quran. Older students studied particular books with individual scholars at mosques such as Sankore or in their homes, reading, discussing and copying texts. When a teacher judged that a student had mastered a book he gave an ijaza, a certificate authorising the student to teach it; students collected several over many years.

questions.question: Name five subjects studied in Timbuktu and explain why its scholarship is important evidence today.
questions.expected_answer: Subjects: Islamic religion, law and government, mathematics, astronomy, medicine, history, geography, grammar and poetry. It is important because it proves that West Africa had a long tradition of written scholarship, disproving colonial claims that Africa had no history or learning before Europeans.
